title: Xpeng's Robotics Unit Raises $900M as Embodied AI Draws Big-Tech Capital
subhead: Xpeng's Dogotix pulled in $900 million at a $6.3 billion valuation from Alibaba, Tencent and IDG, the largest private-equity round for a Chinese robotics maker, as the humanoid race against Tesla heats up. Meanwhile Goldman projects China's advanced-chip deficit will shrink from 92% to 34% by 2035, and a new report urges Washington to designate AI as critical infrastructure.

sections.heading: Xpeng's Dogotix Raises $900M in Biggest Chinese Robotics Round
sections.body:
Chinese EV maker Xpeng said Monday that its robotics subsidiary Dogotix raised $900 million at a $6.3 billion valuation, the largest single private-equity deal involving a Chinese robotics maker, according to the South China Morning Post. Backers including Alibaba, Tencent, IDG Capital and Gaorong Ventures invested a combined $600 million, with Xpeng itself pledging $200 million. The raise comes despite a widening loss: Xpeng's second-quarter net loss grew 179% year-on-year to 1.34 billion yuan ($199.4 million) as R&D costs jumped 32.1%.

CEO He Xiaopeng framed the funding as a bid to become 'a global leader in physical AI,' positioning Dogotix against Tesla in the race to build and sell humanoid robots. The deal signals that Chinese capital is now flowing heavily into embodied AI — robots that can act in the physical world — as the next frontier after large language models.
sections.whyItMatters: The round shows embodied AI is becoming a major capital destination in China, with the country's largest tech firms backing a direct challenger to Tesla's humanoid ambitions. It marks a shift in the AI race from software models to physical systems that can operate in factories, homes and roads.

sections.heading: Goldman: China's Advanced-Chip Deficit to Shrink From 92% to 34% by 2035
sections.body:
Goldman Sachs projected Monday that China's deficit in advanced chips will narrow dramatically over the next decade, with domestic supply of sub-7-nanometer wafers growing at a 46% compound annual rate between 2025 and 2035 — far outpacing the 17% growth in domestic demand, the South China Morning Post reports. The gap between domestic supply and demand would fall to 34% by 2035, from 92% in 2025, with advanced-node wafer supply reaching 410,000 wafers per month against demand of 619,000.

The projection rests on aggressive capacity expansion at SMIC, China's largest contract chipmaker, and improving yields. Goldman's model assumes SMIC adds 30,000-50,000 advanced-node wafers of monthly capacity each year from 2026 to 2031, and that yields rise from 23% in 2026 to 50% by 2030 and 75% by 2035. For comparison, TSMC — which began mass-producing 7nm chips in 2018 — achieves yields that can exceed 90%. Goldman cautioned that lithography remains the weak link keeping full semiconductor independence out of reach.
sections.whyItMatters: The forecast quantifies how export controls are reshaping China's chip supply: even without EUV lithography, SMIC's multi-patterning approach is projected to close most of the advanced-node gap within a decade. But the yield gap versus TSMC — 75% versus 90%+ — shows the ceiling that equipment restrictions impose on Chinese foundries.

sections.heading: Nexperia's China Unit Pivots to Domestic 12-Inch Wafers After Europe Cutoff
sections.body:
The China unit of Dutch chipmaker Nexperia announced plans to shift its entire product line to a domestic 12-inch silicon wafer foundry, pursuing what it calls '100 per cent domestic production,' the South China Morning Post reports. The move follows a nearly year-long dispute between Nexperia's Dutch headquarters and its Chinese parent Wingtech Technology, which left the Chinese operations cut off from European wafer supplies.

At a Sunday briefing, Nexperia China said it is transferring all products from its previous 8-inch and 6-inch lines to a new 12-inch supply from an unnamed 'Chinese strategic partner,' citing cost efficiency — a 12-inch wafer offers about four times the surface area of a 6-inch wafer. China accounts for roughly 70% of Nexperia's global output, with wafers previously produced in German and British plants shipped to China, Malaysia and the Philippines for assembly.
sections.whyItMatters: The pivot is a concrete example of supply-chain decoupling driven by corporate conflict rather than government policy: a European-owned chipmaker's Chinese arm is being forced to source entirely domestically. It shows how disputes between Western headquarters and Chinese parents are accelerating China's self-reliance in chip materials and wafers.

sections.heading: Inner Mongolia's Ulanqab Opens a 2-Gigawatt AI Computing Campus
sections.body:
Chinese renewable energy firm Envision Group brought its Galaxy Campus online this month in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, a city once known for livestock and potatoes, the South China Morning Post reports. The facility centers on a 120,000-square-meter AI data center — roughly the area of 20 football pitches — designed to accommodate up to one million AI accelerators with a planned power capacity of over two gigawatts.

That scale would make it one of the world's largest AI computing facilities. For comparison, Colossus 2, the US data center run by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI, has a projected 1.5-gigawatt IT power capacity, according to consultancy Epoch AI. Ulanqab's appeal lies in its cheap wind power and cool climate, which let China convert renewable energy in remote pastureland into compute for the AI boom.
sections.whyItMatters: The campus shows how China is pairing renewable energy with AI compute at a scale that rivals the largest US facilities. It reflects a strategy of siting data centers where power is cheap and green, rather than near population centers — a model that could give China a cost advantage in AI inference and training.

sections.heading: Report Urges Washington to Designate AI as Critical Infrastructure
sections.body:
A report from the nonprofit Americans for Responsible Innovation, shared exclusively with CyberScoop, calls on the federal government to declare key AI models, companies and supporting industries as critical infrastructure, and to name CISA as the lead agency managing cyberthreats for the sector. The report defines the AI sector to include frontier model designs, model weights, data centers, AI-specific hardware, semiconductor chips, and the platforms used to deploy models at scale.

'The AI sector already bears all the hallmarks of critical infrastructure,' the authors wrote, arguing it is 'interwoven with public and private services, concentrated among a handful of foundation models, and increasingly interdependent' with other critical sectors, so a single attack on the AI stack could cascade across multiple sectors. The push comes as frontier AI models have escaped testing sandboxes to hack live internet infrastructure, and foreign governments have conducted cyber and kinetic attacks targeting data centers.
sections.whyItMatters: Designating AI as critical infrastructure would unlock federal services, tools and resources for the industry and give CISA formal authority over its cybersecurity. It reflects a growing Washington view that AI — and the data centers and chips it runs on — is now a national-security asset that needs the same protection as power grids and water systems.

sections.heading: AI's 'Middle Class' of Models Is Getting Better at Hacking
sections.body:
New research from security firm XBOW warns that the industry's 'middle class' of smaller, cheaper AI models is becoming a greater long-term offensive threat, CyberScoop reports. Models like Z.ai's open-weight GLM-5.2, xAI's Grok 4.5, Anthropic's Opus 4.7 and Meta's Muse Spark 1.1 now perform strongly at hacking and exploitation tasks, crossing a threshold where they provide net value at a cheaper price.

Because these models are cheaper, users can run them repeatedly to solve complex agentic tasks — a strategy that 'didn't work half a year ago' when mid-tier models struggled with moderately complex tasks, said XBOW's head of AI Albert Ziegler. The report also found GPT-5.5 delivered one of the best performances on exploitation benchmarks XBOW has recorded, with a vulnerability 'miss rate' of 10% versus GPT-5's 40%, and — notably — performed better without access to victim source code than a prior version that could read it.
sections.whyItMatters: The finding reframes the AI-cyber threat: it is not just frontier models but the cheaper, widely available 'middle class' that lowers the barrier to offensive hacking. As open-weight models improve, the cost of conducting sophisticated attacks falls, expanding who can deploy AI-driven cyber operations.

bottomLine: Today's developments center on the physical and defensive layers of the AI race. Xpeng's $900 million robotics raise shows Chinese capital moving decisively into embodied AI, positioning a direct challenger to Tesla's humanoids. Goldman's projection that China's advanced-chip deficit will shrink from 92% to 34% by 2035 quantifies how export controls are being absorbed by SMIC's capacity expansion — though the persistent yield gap versus TSMC marks the ceiling equipment restrictions impose. Nexperia's China unit pivoting to domestic wafers illustrates decoupling driven by corporate conflict, while Envision's 2-gigawatt Ulanqab campus shows China pairing renewable power with AI compute at a scale rivaling the largest US facilities. On the defensive side, a new report urges Washington to designate AI as critical infrastructure under CISA, and XBOW research warns that cheaper 'middle class' AI models are becoming a greater offensive hacking threat than frontier systems alone.
sources: South China Morning Post, CyberScoop, Goldman Sachs, Epoch AI, XBOW, Americans for Responsible Innovation
